questions.question: Long before Europeans arrived, the largest Indigenous nation in South Carolina's mountain Upcountry was the:
questions.correctAnswer: Cherokee, whose towns lined the rivers of the southern Appalachian Mountains
distractors: Catawba, whose towns lined the rivers of the southern Appalachian Mountains
Sioux, whose towns lined the rivers of the southern Appalachian Mountains
Apache, whose towns lined the rivers of the southern Appalachian Mountains
questions.explanation: The Cherokee were the dominant nation in the Carolina mountains, with towns along the Keowee and other rivers. The Catawba were powerful too, but their homeland was the Piedmont river valleys, not the high mountains.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cherokee in the Carolina peaks - mountains mean Cherokee.

questions.question: The Indigenous nation centered on the Catawba River in the Piedmont, known for pottery and for allying with the colonists, was the:
questions.correctAnswer: Catawba Nation
distractors: Yamasee Nation
Waccamaw Nation
Edisto Nation
questions.explanation: The Catawba lived along the river that still carries their name in the Piedmont. Skilled potters and traders, they generally allied with South Carolina against rival nations, and their descendants still live near Rock Hill today.

questions.question: English settlers founded Charles Towne, the first permanent English settlement in South Carolina, in what year?
questions.correctAnswer: 1670, on the Ashley River at Albemarle Point
distractors: 1607, on the Ashley River at Albemarle Point
1700, on the Ashley River at Albemarle Point
1562, on the Ashley River at Albemarle Point
questions.explanation: Ships from England and Barbados landed settlers in 1670. A decade later the town moved across the river to the Charleston peninsula, between the Ashley and Cooper rivers, where deeper water and better defense served the growing port.

questions.question: South Carolina began as a proprietary colony, which means it was:
questions.correctAnswer: Granted by the king to eight Lords Proprietors who owned and governed it
distractors: Ruled directly by the king's royal governor from the start
Governed by an elected assembly with no English oversight
Owned by a single trading company in London
questions.explanation: In 1663 Charles II granted Carolina to eight loyal supporters, the Lords Proprietors. They recruited settlers and expected profits from land rents and trade. Colonists disliked proprietary rule so much that in 1719 they overthrew it, and by 1729 the colony had split into royal North and South Carolina.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Eight proprietors owned the colony - proprietary means privately granted.

questions.question: Many of South Carolina's earliest English settlers, including many enslavers, came from which Caribbean island colony?
questions.correctAnswer: Barbados
distractors: Jamaica
Cuba
Haiti
questions.explanation: Barbados was crowded and land-poor by the 1660s, so Barbadian planters moved to Carolina bringing their plantation system - and enslaved Africans - with them. That is why early South Carolina, alone among the mainland colonies, was shaped from the start by a Caribbean slave society.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Barbados to Carolina - the plantation system sailed north.

questions.question: South Carolina's harsh slave code was closely modeled on the code of:
questions.correctAnswer: Barbados, brought by Barbadian settlers
distractors: Virginia, copied from the Jamestown assembly
Massachusetts, copied from Puritan law
Spain, copied from Florida's laws
questions.explanation: Because so many founders came from Barbados, Carolina copied its slave code from that island's brutal system, which treated enslaved people as property with almost no legal protection. After the Stono Rebellion, the Negro Act of 1740 tightened this code further, banning literacy and assembly for enslaved people.

questions.question: Rice became South Carolina's richest export mainly because:
questions.correctAnswer: Enslaved West Africans brought expert knowledge of growing rice in flooded fields
distractors: Rice seeds from England grew well with no special skill
Carolina's dry sandy soil was perfect for rice
Proprietors ordered rice grown instead of all other crops
questions.explanation: West Africans from the Rice Coast had grown rice for generations, including building dikes and floodgates to flood fields with river tides. Planters deliberately sought enslaved people from that region, and their knowledge - not just their labor - created the Carolina rice kingdom in the Lowcountry swamps and tidal rivers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The rice know-how crossed the Atlantic with West Africans.

questions.question: Under the task system used on many Lowcountry rice plantations, an enslaved worker who finished the assigned daily task:
questions.correctAnswer: Could use the remaining time to grow food or make goods for their own family
distractors: Was immediately given a second full task by the overseer
Earned wages equal to a free worker's pay
Was allowed to leave the plantation permanently
questions.explanation: Unlike the gang system on cotton plantations, the task system measured work by a set job - for example a quarter-acre of rice field. Finishing early gave enslaved families a little time for their own gardens and crafts, one reason African foodways and skills survived so strongly in Lowcountry Gullah culture.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Finish the task, keep the rest of the day - task system.

questions.question: The Gullah Geechee culture of the Sea Islands and Lowcountry is best described as:
questions.correctAnswer: An African American culture and creole language preserving many West African traditions
distractors: A Native American language spoken in the Upcountry
A German settler dialect from the Dutch Fork
A style of colonial architecture in Charleston
questions.explanation: Isolated on the Sea Islands, enslaved Africans and their descendants blended West African languages, foods, crafts, and beliefs with English into Gullah culture and language. Sweetgrass basket weaving, for example, descends directly from West African coiled basket traditions and is still practiced around Charleston today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gullah Geechee - West Africa kept alive on the Sea Islands.

questions.question: Eliza Lucas Pinckney is famous in colonial South Carolina for:
questions.correctAnswer: Developing indigo as a major export crop in the 1740s
distractors: Founding the city of Charleston
Leading the Regulators in the backcountry
Writing the colony's first newspaper
questions.explanation: As a teenager managing her father's plantations, Eliza Lucas experimented for years until indigo - a plant producing valuable blue dye for British cloth - grew and processed successfully in Carolina. Indigo became the colony's second great export after rice, filling the seasons when rice fields lay idle.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Eliza Lucas made Carolina blue - indigo blue.

questions.question: The Lowcountry and the Upcountry differed in the colonial era mainly because:
questions.correctAnswer: The Lowcountry held wealthy rice plantations worked by enslaved people, while the Upcountry held small farms with few enslaved people
distractors: The Lowcountry was mountainous and the Upcountry was coastal
The Upcountry grew rice and the Lowcountry grew cotton
The Lowcountry had no towns and the Upcountry had the only port
questions.explanation: Tidal rivers made the flat Lowcountry ideal for rice, creating a wealthy planter elite and a Black majority. The hilly Upcountry, settled later by Scots-Irish and German small farmers, had poorer farms and far fewer enslaved people. This split shaped South Carolina politics for two centuries.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Lowcountry rice riches, Upcountry small farms - two Carolinas.

questions.question: In 1739, the Stono Rebellion near Charleston was:
questions.correctAnswer: An uprising of enslaved Africans who seized weapons and marched toward freedom in Spanish Florida
distractors: A tax revolt by Charleston merchants against the Proprietors
A Cherokee attack on the Charles Towne settlement
A mutiny by British soldiers at a coastal fort
questions.explanation: In September 1739, enslaved Africans led by a man remembered as Jemmy rose near the Stono River, seized guns, and headed south - Spain had promised freedom to enslaved people who reached Florida. The militia stopped the march, and the colony answered with the Negro Act of 1740, one of the harshest slave codes in British America.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Stono 1739 - a march south toward Spanish freedom.

questions.question: Spain's offer that inspired enslaved Carolinians like those at Stono was:
questions.correctAnswer: Freedom for enslaved people who escaped to Spanish Florida and converted to Catholicism
distractors: Land in Cuba for any enslaved person who worked ten years
Passage back to Africa on Spanish ships
Gold payments to enslavers who freed their workers
questions.explanation: From St. Augustine, Spain promised liberty to fugitives from the English colonies who accepted Catholicism, and some founded the free Black town of Fort Mose in 1738. News of the offer traveled the coast and helped inspire the Stono marchers, whose goal was Florida, about 150 miles south.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Florida meant freedom - Spain's promise pulled people south.

questions.question: The Yamasee War of 1715 nearly destroyed the young colony because:
questions.correctAnswer: Native nations attacked after years of trade abuses, debt, and enslavement of Native people by colonists
distractors: France armed the Yamasee to conquer Charleston for Louisiana
The Yamasee objected to paying British taxes on tea
A hurricane destroyed the colony's farms the same year
questions.explanation: Carolina traders cheated Native partners, ran them into debt, and enslaved their families. In April 1715 the Yamasee and their allies struck settlements across the colony, killing hundreds. The colony survived with Cherokee help, but the war shattered Native power in the Lowcountry and helped end proprietary rule in 1719.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Trade abuse and enslavement lit the Yamasee War.

questions.question: The Regulator movement of the 1760s in the South Carolina backcountry demanded:
questions.correctAnswer: Courts, law enforcement, and fair representation for Upcountry settlers
distractors: Independence from Britain twenty years early
An end to all taxes on rice exports
A separate colony for the Upcountry with its own king
questions.explanation: Backcountry settlers had no local courts or sheriffs, so horse thieves and outlaw gangs operated freely. The Regulators organized to demand courts and representation - and sometimes took the law into their own hands. The colony finally created circuit courts in 1769, a step toward balancing Lowcountry and Upcountry power.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Regulators wanted rules - courts for the backcountry.

questions.question: Besides rice and indigo, colonial South Carolina earned money exporting naval stores, which were:
questions.correctAnswer: Tar, pitch, and turpentine from pine trees, used to waterproof ships
distractors: Sails and ropes woven from palmetto fibers
Fresh fish packed for Caribbean markets
Iron tools forged in Charleston workshops
questions.explanation: Britain's navy needed tar and pitch to seal wooden ships, and Carolina's longleaf pines supplied them, along with a busy trade in deerskins from the interior. These forest exports mattered most in areas unsuited to rice, connecting backcountry hunters and Native traders to Atlantic markets.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pine made ships waterproof - tar, pitch, turpentine.

questions.question: In 1719, South Carolinians overthrew the Lords Proprietors and asked the king to take over mainly because:
questions.correctAnswer: The Proprietors had failed to protect the colony during the Yamasee War and pirate attacks
distractors: The Proprietors banned the growing of rice
The king offered to end slavery in the colony
The Proprietors moved the capital to London
questions.explanation: During the Yamasee War and pirate raids on Charleston, the Proprietors sent little help while demanding quitrents. The assembly declared proprietary rule ended and petitioned for royal government. By 1729 Carolina was formally two royal colonies, North and South - a split that also settled the old joint grant.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No protection, no proprietors - 1719 turned royal.

questions.question: Charleston's location between the Ashley and Cooper rivers mattered because the two rivers:
questions.correctAnswer: Form a fine harbor where, as locals say, they meet to form the Atlantic Ocean
distractors: Created a waterfall used to power textile mills
Marked the border between North and South Carolina
Supplied fresh drinking water to rice fields inland
questions.explanation: Moved to the peninsula in 1680, Charleston sat on one of the best natural harbors on the Atlantic coast. Ships loaded rice, indigo, and deerskins there, making Charleston the fourth-largest city in colonial British America and the main port of entry for enslaved Africans in North America.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ashley plus Cooper equals Charleston's harbor.

questions.question: A large share of enslaved Africans brought to North America entered through:
questions.correctAnswer: Charleston harbor, including Sullivan's Island, its quarantine station
distractors: Beaufort, on Port Royal Sound
Georgetown, on Winyah Bay
Columbia, on the Congaree River
questions.explanation: Historians estimate around 40 percent of enslaved Africans who survived the crossing to mainland North America arrived through Charleston, first held in pest houses on Sullivan's Island. The site is now part of the International African American Museum story, opened on Gadsden's Wharf in Charleston in 2023.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sullivan's Island - the Ellis Island of Black America, in sorrow.

questions.question: By the mid-1700s, South Carolina's Lowcountry was unusual in British North America because:
questions.correctAnswer: Enslaved Africans and their descendants formed the majority of the population
distractors: Most residents were free German farmers
It had banned slavery within the Charleston city limits
Its population was evenly split among ten Native nations
questions.explanation: Rice planters imported so many enslaved Africans that Black Carolinians outnumbered white colonists in the Lowcountry - at times roughly two to one. That majority is a core reason African language, food, craft, and religious traditions shaped Lowcountry culture so deeply, from Gullah speech to rice cuisine.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In the Lowcountry, the majority was African - culture followed.

questions.question: When Parliament passed the Stamp Act in 1765, Charleston protesters were led in part by:
questions.correctAnswer: Christopher Gadsden, a merchant who became a leading Patriot voice
distractors: Francis Marion, the Swamp Fox partisan leader
William Bull, the royal lieutenant governor
Denmark Vesey, a free Black carpenter
questions.explanation: Gadsden organized resistance through the Sons of Liberty in Charleston, where stamps were locked in Fort Johnson and never used. He later represented South Carolina in the Continental Congress. His famous rattlesnake flag came later, in 1775, as naval commander-in-chief Esek Hopkins adopted his design.

questions.question: Charleston's response to the Tea Act in 1773 differed from Boston's because Charlestonians:
questions.correctAnswer: Refused to buy the tea and stored it in a damp warehouse, where much of it spoiled
distractors: Dumped all the tea into Charleston harbor in one night
Burned the tea ship at its dock
Shipped the tea back to London the same day
questions.explanation: Charleston held mass meetings, forced the tea consignees to resign, and let the tea sit unloaded in the Exchange basement for three years rather than paying the tax. Some was later sold to fund the Patriot war effort. Boston destroyed tea; Charleston, characteristically, out-waited it.

questions.question: The palmetto tree appears on South Carolina's flag because, at the Battle of Sullivan's Island in 1776:
questions.correctAnswer: Cannonballs bounced off or sank harmlessly into the fort's soft palmetto-log walls
distractors: Palmetto fronds were used to build the fort's gunpowder magazine
A palmetto tree hid the fort's commander from British snipers
Sailors carved the victory date into a palmetto trunk
questions.explanation: Colonel William Moultrie's unfinished fort was built of palmetto logs packed with sand. On June 28, 1776, British cannon fire thudded harmlessly into the spongy wood while the fort's guns crippled the fleet - the first major Patriot victory of the war in the South. The palmetto and crescent from Moultrie's flag became the state flag.

questions.question: June 28, the anniversary of the 1776 victory at Sullivan's Island, is celebrated in South Carolina as:
questions.correctAnswer: Carolina Day
distractors: Palmetto Independence Day only in Charleston
Moultrie Day in the Upcountry
Founders Day across the state
questions.explanation: Carolina Day marks the Sullivan's Island victory, won a week before the Declaration of Independence was announced. questions.question: South Carolina's four signers of the Declaration of Independence were:
questions.correctAnswer: Edward Rutledge, Thomas Heyward Jr., Thomas Lynch Jr., and Arthur Middleton
distractors: John Rutledge, Rawlins Lowndes, Charles Pinckney, and Pierce Butler
Francis Marion, Thomas Sumter, Andrew Pickens, and William Moultrie
Christopher Gadsden, Henry Laurens, John Laurens, and William Henry Drayton
questions.explanation: All four signers were young Lowcountry planters; Edward Rutledge, at 26, was the youngest signer of the Declaration. Thomas Lynch Jr. was lost at sea in 1779. All four were later captured when Charleston fell in 1780 and held as prisoners - a reminder of how completely the war engulfed South Carolina.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rutledge, Heyward, Lynch, Middleton - four Carolina names.

questions.question: The fall of Charleston in May 1780 was a disaster for the Patriot cause because:
questions.correctAnswer: The British captured an entire American army - the worst American defeat of the Revolution
distractors: The state government voted to rejoin Britain permanently
Washington's main army was captured with the city
France withdrew from the war in response
questions.explanation: After a siege, General Benjamin Lincoln surrendered Charleston and more than 5,000 soldiers. Britain then set up posts across the state, expecting Loyalists to hold it. Instead, the occupation - and British abuses - pushed many Carolinians into a brutal civil war between Patriots and Loyalists.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Charleston 1780 - an army surrendered, then the real fight began.

questions.question: Francis Marion earned the nickname 'Swamp Fox' by:
questions.correctAnswer: Leading partisan fighters who struck British units, then vanished into Lowcountry swamps
distractors: Building a fort entirely inside a cypress swamp
Training foxes to carry messages between camps
Defeating the British navy at Georgetown
questions.explanation: Marion's partisans used local knowledge of rivers and swamps around the Pee Dee to ambush supply lines and disappear before British troops could respond.
